title: A Atlas for the Clock
premise: In 1913, Zephyrine Nakamura, a half-Japanese nurse in a coastal garrison town, keeps a private ledger recording the names of soldiers whose deaths the officers' reports omit. When war comes and the army requisitions both the town and her records, she discovers the ledger has been entered as evidence of sedition, and that the man who taught her to keep it—her former patient and quiet love, Elias, now conscripted for the enemy side—is listed among those declared traitors. As the century turns toward open war, Zephyrine must smuggle the true ledger out of occupied territory to fulfill a peacetime promise: that no name would be lost while either of them lived. The novel ends with her delivering the names to a neutral archive at the border on New Year's Eve, choosing memory over safety, and learning Elias survived—not as a soldier, but as a man who kept his own copy of every name.
about_author: Paloma Brightwater is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters in municipal repositories across Europe. She writes historical fiction about the people official records forget, and lives near the sea with an unreasonable number of fountain pens.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Names
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. In the garrison hospital of Saint-Aubin, she begins recording in a cloth-bound ledger the names of dead soldiers struck from official reports—starting with a boy no older than seventeen. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: history happens elsewhere, she tells herself, but her hands say otherwise. Establishes her double life as invisible nurse and secret chronicler.

chapters.title: A Promise Made in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, with flashback. Elias Verhoeven, a foreign cartographer recovering from fever, teaches her map-making and helps her organize the ledger by regiment and date. They make a pact: whoever survives keeps the names. The beat is tender, doomed intimacy—love acknowledged only obliquely, because duty forbids it.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. War arrives not with shells but with paperwork: the army requisitions the town, the hospital, and all documents within it. An intelligence officer, Major Corliss, catalogs her effects—and pauses over the ledger. The beat is dread; the ordinary world ends in ink stamps and inventory lists.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Zephyrine and Corliss. Corliss reads the ledger as evidence: names of enemy nationals, coded geography, a foreigner's handwriting. Zephyrine realizes her act of remembrance has been reclassified as treason. The beat is vertigo—the same object, two irreconcilable meanings.

chapters.title: Declared Enemy
chapters.summary: Elias's POV, from across the border. Conscripted into his home country's army despite years abroad, he learns his name appears on a captured list of suspected collaborators—his own maps used against him. He begins keeping a second ledger. The beat is bitter irony: the record meant to save him now condemns him.

chapters.title: The Interrogation Room
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Corliss offers a bargain: testify against Elias in exchange for leniency. She refuses without drama, simply repeating the names of the dead like a rosary. The beat is moral clarity under pressure—her identity crystallizes around what she will not surrender.

chapters.title: Flight Through Occupied Country
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. With help from the hospital's laundress, Madame Okafor, Zephyrine smuggles the original ledger out sewn into a mattress, traveling with refugees. Elias deserts his post to intercept the border road. Rising tension peaks: both are hunted, both are carrying the same promise in different directions.

chapters.title: The Bridge at Varennes
chapters.summary: Dual climax POV. On a frozen bridge, Zephyrine and Elias meet by accident—or design—moments before a patrol does. To save each other they split the ledger: she takes the names, he takes the maps proving where the omissions were ordered. The beat is sacrifice made concrete; love expressed as division of labor, not embrace.

chapters.title: Century's End
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. On New Year's Eve, she reaches the neutral archive at the border, half-frozen, and reads all three hundred names aloud so they enter the record as testimony, not just paper. Corliss arrives—but chooses, ambiguously, to log her statement as 'civilian deposition' rather than arrest her. The beat is catharsis: memory wins a small, permanent victory.

chapters.title: An Atlas for the Clock
chapters.summary: Epilogue, alternating POV, spring 1914. Elias finds her in the rebuilt town carrying his own ledger; the two books, compared page by page, match. They begin drawing a new map—one marked not by borders but by graves and promises kept. The final beat is resolution: identity reclaimed, love chosen over duty, and time itself made accountable to the names.
